en.example: Take a paper rectangle with two rows of four equal squares. The whole has 8 squares. Shade one row: 4 of 8 squares are shaded, so 4/8 = 1/2. On a second rectangle with two rows of six equal squares, one row is 6/12 = 1/2. The shaded areas can have different sizes, yet each is half of its own whole. On a number line from 0 to 1, both fractions occupy the midpoint, because the unit is now the same. en.example: Compare two fictional boats: A has a broad, shallow hull; B has a narrow, deep hull. Record both using the same criteria—width and depth—rather than listing unrelated features such as A’s colour and B’s name. The description now supports questions about where each could travel. A shallow-water route makes depth relevant, but actual suitability also depends on the water and the boat’s requirements. Organized comparison selects criteria because they help answer a question.
en.question: Would saying “A is better because it is wider” complete the comparison?
en.answer: No. Better for what purpose and conditions? Specify the question, then relate the relevant feature to it. Comparison develops understanding when it connects features and functions, not when it turns a difference into an unexplained ranking.

en.example: Use invented records of a toy cart: on the same surface, released from rest at a low ramp mark it travels 40 cm; from a higher mark it travels 70 cm. The changed release height is a plausible cause because it changes the starting condition; the longer travel is the result. Repeated trials and keeping the cart, surface and release method comparable would strengthen the comparison. One pair of distances does not isolate every influence or supply a complete mechanism.
en.question: If the second run also uses a smoother floor, can the extra distance be attributed only to height?
en.answer: No. Height and surface changed together. Compare one relevant condition at a time where possible and explain the proposed mechanism. A causal explanation needs more than noticing that two numbers differ; reasoning about this is not restricted to one birthday.

pt.example: Use registros inventados de um carrinho: na mesma superfície, solto do repouso numa marca baixa de uma rampa, percorre 40 cm; de uma marca mais alta, 70 cm. pt.answer: Explique a razão da decisão, acolha perguntas pertinentes e mantenha expectativas claras e justas. A finalidade é compreender e exercitar responsabilidade, além de apenas aceitar ou rejeitar a autoridade.

en.example: A project must be displayed on Friday. Pupils ask to submit everything on Friday morning. The teacher explains that mounting takes a day and feedback another day, so a Wednesday draft serves the shared deadline. Pupils can choose their internal work schedule while retaining that dependency. Authority supplies a reason and a boundary; pupils gain a real area of responsibility rather than a choice that makes the plan impossible.
en.question: If the display moves to Monday, must Wednesday remain unquestionable to preserve authority?
en.answer: No. Reconsider the schedule in light of the changed reason, while keeping enough time for feedback and mounting. Revising an explained rule can show consistency of purpose. It is not the same as abandoning every expectation.

en.example: A fictional class considers moving a club from Tuesday to Thursday. Twelve members were asked: eight can attend Tuesday and six Thursday. That supports Tuesday for those respondents, but says nothing yet about four members who were absent. A reasoned conclusion can be provisional: retain Tuesday while asking the missing members. Independence lies in explaining the evidence and its limit, even if the conclusion agrees with the teacher.
en.question: If the four absent members can attend only Thursday, does the earlier count stay decisive?
en.answer: No. The relevant totals become eight for Tuesday and ten for Thursday, assuming the earlier answers remain unchanged. Revising the conclusion follows the stated criterion. Keeping the first answer merely to appear independent would confuse stubbornness with judgment.

pt.example: Uma turma fictícia considera mudar um clube de terça para quinta. Consultaram doze membros: oito podem na terça e seis na quinta. Isso favorece terça entre os respondentes, mas nada informa sobre quatro ausentes. Uma conclusão fundamentada pode ser provisória: manter terça enquanto se consulta quem faltou. Independência está em explicar evidência e limite, mesmo concordando com a professora.
pt.question: Se os quatro ausentes só podem na quinta, a contagem anterior continua decisiva?

en.example: A pupil solves 18 + 27 quickly. A deeper task asks for two methods: 18 + 20 + 7 = 45, or 20 + 25 = 45 after transferring 2 from one addend to the other. en.example: A child shades three of six equal squares and says, “It is half because three shaded and three unshaded make equal shares.” The drawing represents the relationship, and the explanation identifies it. Rearranging the shaded squares without changing their number preserves 3/6. Art helps make a comparison visible here; the concept does not depend on using a particular colour or drawing beautifully.

en.question: For a triangle with sides 4, 4 and 6, what would demonstrate transfer?
en.answer: Adding all three boundary lengths, 4 + 4 + 6 = 14, and explaining that both equal sides count. Saying “I used the book” identifies a resource, not the reasoning. Ask how the resource changed the explanation.

pt.example: O caderno de um aluno identifica um triângulo de lados 3, 4 e 5 e chama seu perímetro de 7. Uma referência define perímetro como comprimento total do contorno. O aluno percorre os três lados e corrige para 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. O registro pessoal mostra ideia inicial e correção; a referência oferece uma definição para conferir. Possuir a referência ou copiar sua página não explicaria por que a primeira resposta omitiu um lado.
pt.question: Num triângulo de lados 4, 4 e 6, o que demonstraria transferência?
pt.answer: Somar os três comprimentos do contorno, 4 + 4 + 6 = 14, explicando que ambos os lados iguais contam. Dizer “usei o livro” identifica um recurso, não o raciocínio. Pergunte como o recurso mudou a explicação.

audit.learningObjective: Compare the roles of pupil-created records and independent references.
essentialConcepts: A pupil-created lesson book can require selecting, organizing and explaining ideas. Its value depends on what the pupil understands, not simply on making a neat copy of the teacher’s page.
Textbooks and reference materials offer another explanation, structured practice and information pupils can check independently. These roles can complement a classroom-created record.

Ask how accuracy is corrected, how pupils find information and how learners who need accessible formats are supported. A reduced reliance on one textbook should not mean reduced access to dependable explanations or adequate practice.
audit.prerequisite: Add all boundary lengths and distinguish a reference from evidence of understanding.

Neither merely owning the reference nor copying its page would show why the first answer omitted a side.
